summary: Describes a simple mechanism for detecting data plane failures in MPLS Label Switched Paths. It has two parts: the information in an MPLS echo request and echo reply used for fault detection and isolation, and ways to send the reply reliably. It is standards-track and was replaced by RFC 8029.

plainLanguage.summary: Like ping for a label-switched path: send a small hello down the path and see whether an answer comes back.

subtitle: Ping and traceroute for MPLS label switched paths, run through the data plane itself.

tldr.problem: When an MPLS label switched path (LSP) fails to deliver traffic, the control plane cannot always notice. Operators need a way to find such black holes and misrouting, and to locate the fault.
tldr.mechanism: A router sends an MPLS echo request, a UDP packet that names the path under test (its FEC stack) and travels the same data path as ordinary traffic. The router that receives it checks it against its control plane and returns an echo reply with a return code.
tldr.outcome: The tool works in a ping mode (end-to-end check) and a traceroute mode (hop-by-hop fault isolation). RFC 4379 was later obsoleted by RFC 8029.

today: RFC 4379 is a Proposed Standard that has been obsoleted by RFC 8029, which is the current specification. It was also updated by RFC 5462, RFC 6424, RFC 6425, RFC 6426, RFC 6829, RFC 7506, RFC 7537 and RFC 7743.

sections.title: Why Test the Data Plane
sections.content:
An LSP can fail to deliver user traffic without the MPLS control plane noticing. RFC 4379 gives operators a tool to detect such traffic black holes or misrouting within a reasonable time, and a mechanism to isolate the fault. It is modeled on ping and traceroute: a ping mode is a basic connectivity check, and a traceroute mode is hop-by-hop fault isolation.

The idea is to verify that packets of a particular Forwarding Equivalence Class (FEC) really end their MPLS path on a router that is an egress for that FEC. The test packet, an MPLS echo request, is forwarded just like any other packet of that FEC. In ping mode it is handed to the control plane of the egress router, which checks that it is indeed an egress. In traceroute mode each transit router checks that it is a transit router for the path.

The echo request is routed only by its label stack, never by its IP destination address. For this reason the RFC makes a special use of the address range 127/8, an exception to RFC 1122 that the RFC says it updates. Such packets should be discarded by hosts, and routers should not IP-forward them, so a diagnostic packet that escapes a broken LSP is unlikely to reach a user.
sections.plainLanguage: Sometimes a road looks fine on the map but cars still never arrive. This tool sends a test car down the real road to see where it really ends up.

sections.title: The Echo Request and Reply Packet
sections.content:
An echo request is a possibly labeled IPv4 or IPv6 UDP packet. Its payload starts with fixed fields: Version Number (currently 1), Global Flags, Message Type (1 for echo request, 2 for echo reply), Reply Mode, Return Code, Return Subcode, a Sender's Handle, a Sequence Number, and two timestamps in NTP format (sent and received). Variable-length TLVs follow.

The only global flag defined is the V bit. When it is 1, the sender wants the receiver to validate the FEC stack; when it is 0, the choice is left to the receiver. The reply mode tells the receiver how to answer: do not reply (1), reply via an IPv4/IPv6 UDP packet (2), reply via a UDP packet with Router Alert (3), or reply via an application level control channel (4).

The receiver puts a return code in its reply. Examples are 1 (malformed echo request), 3 (the replying router is an egress for the FEC at the stated stack depth) and 4 (no mapping for the FEC at that depth). The return subcode carries the stack depth for codes that specify one.
sections.plainLanguage: The test packet has a form with boxes: who sent it, which number it is, what time it left, and how to reply. The answer fills in a box saying what the router found.

sections.title: TLVs and the Target FEC Stack
sections.content:
Extra information travels in TLVs (type, length, value). Types below 32768 are mandatory: an implementation must support them or return code 2 (one or more TLVs not understood). Types of 32768 and above are optional and should be ignored if not understood. The top-level types include Target FEC Stack (1), Downstream Mapping (2), Pad (3), Vendor Enterprise Number (5), Interface and Label Stack (7), Errored TLVs (9) and Reply TOS Byte (10).

Every echo request must carry a Target FEC Stack that describes the path being tested. The stack is a list of sub-TLVs, with the first FEC matching the top of the label stack. The RFC defines sub-types for LDP and RSVP prefixes and tunnels, VPN prefixes, L2 VPN endpoints, pseudowires, BGP labeled prefixes, generic prefixes and a Nil FEC for reserved labels such as Router Alert and Explicit-null.

In traceroute mode the request should also include a Downstream Mapping TLV. It describes the downstream interface and labels, and lets a router report how traffic could be forwarded over each equal-cost path.
sections.plainLanguage: The note inside the toy train says which road it is supposed to be testing. Extra notes can ask each station to tell you which road comes next.

sections.title: How Ping and Traceroute Work
sections.content:
The sender builds a UDP packet with a routable source address and a destination chosen at random from 127/8 (or the IPv6 form 0:0:0:0:0:FFFF:127/104). The IP TTL is 1, the destination UDP port is 3503, and the Router Alert option must be set. It is sent with the label stack that matches the FEC stack. In ping mode the TTL of the outermost label is 255. In traceroute mode it is set to 1, then 2, and so on.

A router receives the packet in its control plane because of an exception such as the Router Alert option, a TTL expiring, or a 127/8 destination, and identifies it by UDP port 3503. It checks that the packet is well formed, then walks the label stack and validates labels and, if requested, the FEC stack. It picks the best return code, such as 8 (label switched at this depth), 3 (egress for the FEC), 11 (no label entry) or 10 (mapping for this FEC is not the given label), and sends an echo reply.

The echo reply is a UDP packet with the IP TTL set to 255. It copies the sender's handle, sequence number and sent timestamp from the request, and its destination is the request's source address and port. The original sender matches the reply to a request by destination UDP port and handle, then checks the sequence number. To trace further, it copies any returned Downstream Mappings into its next request with the TTL raised by one.

Because paths may use equal-cost multipath, the sender can vary the destination address and source port, and use the multipath information in Downstream Mapping, to exercise more paths. The RFC admits that full coverage may not be possible. If a router does not support the tool, no reply arrives and the sender may probe further hops.
sections.plainLanguage: The test train goes one station further each time. Each station answers, so you learn where the track stops working.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says the security needs are similar to those of ICMP ping. It names three kinds of attack: denial of service by flooding routers with echo requests or replies, tampering with or spoofing replies to hide the real state of the data plane, and an unauthorized party using the tool to learn about the network.

Implementations are RECOMMENDED to apply a rate limiter to the well-known UDP port and to check the source address of echo requests against an access list. They should also be able to filter the addresses to which replies may be sent. Simple spoofed replies are unlikely to work, since they must match the handle and sequence number of an outstanding request, and an implementation MAY also require an exact match on the sent timestamp.

The 127/8 range is used only together with UDP port 3503. A router that receives a 127/8 packet with another destination port must treat it as RFC 1812 requires, which by default means as a martian.
sections.plainLanguage: Because anyone could knock on the test door, routers should limit how often they answer and only answer people they know.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content:
IANA allocated TCP and UDP port 3503 for LSP echo requests and replies. The RFC also asks IANA to keep registries for Message Types, Reply Modes and Return Codes, each with values from 0 to 255. Values 0 to 191 are assigned by Standards Action, 192 to 251 by Specification Required, and 252 to 255 are for vendor private use.

When any of these fields falls in the vendor private range, a Vendor Enterprise Number TLV must be present in the message. A further registry covers the TLV types and sub-types.
sections.plainLanguage: A global list keeps track of which numbers mean what, so everyone's tools speak the same language.

items.label: No return code
items.desc: Set by the sender in a request.

items.label: Malformed echo request
items.desc: The request was not well formed.

items.label: TLV not understood
items.desc: One or more TLVs were not understood.

items.label: Egress for the FEC
items.desc: Replying router is an egress at the stated stack depth.

items.label: No mapping
items.desc: Replying router has no mapping for the FEC at that depth.

items.label: Label switched
items.desc: Label switched at the stated stack depth.

items.label: No MPLS forwarding
items.desc: Label switched but no MPLS forwarding at that depth.

items.label: Mapping is not the label
items.desc: Mapping for this FEC is not the given label.

items.label: No label entry
items.desc: No label entry at the stated stack depth.

items.label: Protocol mismatch
items.desc: Protocol not associated with interface at that depth.

items.label: Premature termination
items.desc: Label stack shrank to a single label.
